subject: the Barbican Estate, City of London (Chamberlin, Powell and Bon)
guess: Unidentified modern religious or civic complex: a slender freestanding tower (bell tower or minaret) at one corner beside a low barrel-vaulted hall with a glazed atrium, colonnade and reflecting pool. It is possibly a mosque-and-minaret group in the spirit of Hassan II Mosque, but nothing confirms a specific landmark.
strengths: The tall, slender tower is a strong vertical counterpoint to the low hall, and its stepped crown gives a recognisable silhouette.
Repeated ledges and inset trans-clear panels give the tower a convincing rhythm of floors or openings at this scale.
The curved slopes on the hall read clearly as a vaulted or arched roof.
The reflecting pool, colonnade and small glazed atrium add layered landscape and entrance detail on the front side.
The model stays in the Architecture-style white and trans-clear palette.
problems: The subject is not identifiable; nothing in the massing or detailing pins it to a specific real building, which an official set must do.
The base outline is ragged: perimeter tiles stick out unevenly and the border is broken at corners, so it lacks a clean display plinth.
The rear and side elevations of the hall are large blank, lumpy walls, so the model only works from one view.
The tower's ledges look jagged and busy rather than crisp, and the tower barely connects to the hall compositionally.
The hall massing has abrupt, unexplained height changes and scattered small details that read as clutter rather than architecture.
The trans-clear pool infill is patchy, and the dark recesses under the hall look like gaps rather than intended shadow lines.
At 601 pieces, much of the count goes to fiddly paving and base filler instead of defining the building's key features.
issues: Tower proportions (all views): the single tower is a pencil-thin square shaft about ten times taller than it is wide, so it reads as a minaret or campanile. The Cromwell, Shakespeare and Lauderdale towers are broad and triangular in plan. Widen the footprint to a triangular or stepped plan at least 5–6 studs across, and cut the height-to-width ratio to roughly 4–5:1.

Tower crown (View 1/4 top): the rounded, cowled cap reads as a lantern or minaret finial. Replace it with the Barbican's serrated crest: upturned, angled slabs rising in a sawtooth from each face (slopes or wedge plates angled up).

Tower balconies: the small evenly spaced ledges look like decorative bands. The Barbican's identity comes from deep balconies cantilevered from every face, giving a jagged, ribbed silhouette. Make each floor slab project further and stagger them on all three faces.

Only one tower: the estate is defined by three towers rising over long terraces. Even at this scale, add at least a second tower, offset across the lake, or reduce the scale so the trio fits. A lone tower beside a hall is what made the reviewer think 'mosque and minaret'.

Terrace block (Views 2/3): it reads as a short, solid masonry hall with brick-like coursing and no openings. Barbican terraces such as Gilbert House and Ben Jonson House are long, low slabs with continuous horizontal balcony bands, planter troughs and a barrel-vaulted penthouse roof line. Lengthen the block substantially and replace the plain wall with stacked balcony and planter strips (tiles and grilles). Keep the vaults as a repeated rhythm along the roof.
Pilotis: dark columns are visible under the block in View 2, but they are buried. Raise the terrace onto clearly open round columns so it visibly straddles the water, as Gilbert House spans the lake.

Lake (View 1/4): the small rectangular pool in a dark grey frame reads as a reflecting pool at a mosque or memorial. Enlarge it into the dominant central lake running between the terraces, with stepped edges and the lakeside terrace of the Barbican Centre. The dark 'road' borders around it should go.

Glazed atrium (View 1/4): the glass box at ground level reads as a prayer-hall court or winter garden. The Barbican Conservatory sits high on the Centre's fly tower. Either lift it onto a roof or replace it with the Barbican Centre's stepped lakeside front.
Arched colonnade (View 1): the grey arches read as a cloister or portico. Rework them as the elevated podium highwalk, a flat raised walkway on columns linking the blocks above street level.

Missing anchor: add St Giles' Cripplegate, the small Gothic church with a square tower sitting in the water garden. Its contrast with the concrete is one of the most recognisable Barbican views and would immediately fix the location.
verdict: The model carries a few genuine Barbican cues: barrel-vaulted roofs, a tower with balcony bands, water and pilotis. But the composition of one minaret-thin tower beside a compact vaulted hall, an atrium and a formal pool reads as a religious or civic complex, which is exactly what the blind reviewer saw. To be identifiable it needs triangular towers with serrated crowns (ideally more than one), long balconied terrace slabs on pilotis across a large central lake, and St Giles' church as an anchor.
